records.source: Λέγω οὖν, μὴ ἀπώσατο ὁ θεὸς τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ;
records.gloss: I say then, not did reject the God the people of him?
pieces: So I ask: has God rejected {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people?

L.1: I say then, did God reject {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people?

R.1: So I ask this: Has God rejected {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} own people?

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no"
decisions.reason: The question begins with a negative particle that expects a denial, and Paul gives one at once: "May it not be!"

decisions.choice: Psalm 94:14 and 1 Samuel 12:22
decisions.reason: The words echo the promise that God will not reject his people (Psalm 94:14; 1 Samuel 12:22). The Hebrew of both verses has the divine name. Verse 2 turns the question into the answer: "God did not reject his people."

decisions.choice: his people: Israel as the people God chose for himself
decisions.reason: After chapters 9-10, the question is whether Israel's unbelief means God has cast off the nation he chose.

decisions.choice: I ask
decisions.reason: The verb is "I say", but it introduces a question, so Balanced and Readable say "I ask".

records.heading: The remnant of Israel

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο· καὶ γὰρ ἐγὼ Ἰσραηλίτης εἰμί, ἐκ σπέρματος Ἀβραάμ, φυλῆς Βενιαμίν.
records.gloss: Not may it be; also for I an Israelite am, from seed of Abraham, of tribe of Benjamin.
pieces: Certainly not! I myself am an Israelite, descended from Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.

L.1: May it not be! For I also am an Israelite, from [the] seed of Abraham, of [the] tribe of Benjamin.

R.1: Of course not! I am an Israelite too. I come from Abraham's family, from the tribe of Benjamin.

decisions.choice: the strongest possible denial
decisions.reason: μὴ γένοιτο, "may it not happen", is Paul's strongest way of rejecting a false conclusion (3:4, 6:2, 9:14; Galatians 2:17).

decisions.choice: Paul himself is proof that God has not rejected Israel
alternatives: Paul, as an Israelite, could not believe that God would reject his own people
decisions.reason: Paul is a Jew who believes in Jesus, so God has plainly not cast off every Israelite. Verses 2-5 go on to speak of the faithful few in Elijah's day and a remnant now, which fits this reading.

decisions.choice: descended from Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin
decisions.reason: Paul names his descent as he does in Philippians 3:5 and 2 Corinthians 11:22. Benjamin was the tribe of King Saul, whose name Paul also bore.

decisions.choice: descended from Abraham (B); from Abraham's family (R)
decisions.reason: "Seed" means offspring; Balanced and Readable use plain words for it.

decisions.choice: Certainly not! (B); Of course not! (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use ordinary English for an emphatic no. "God forbid" adds a word for God that the Greek does not have.

records.source: οὐκ ἀπώσατο ὁ θεὸς τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ ὃν προέγνω.
records.gloss: Not did reject the God the people of him whom he foreknew.
pieces: God has not rejected {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people, whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} foreknew.

L.2: God did not reject {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people, whom {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} foreknew.

R.2: No, God has not rejected {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} people. He knew them and chose them from the beginning.

decisions.choice: foreknew: knew beforehand in the sense of choosing them as his own
alternatives: knew in advance what they would do
decisions.reason: In Scripture God's "knowing" a people often means choosing them in love (Amos 3:2), and in 8:29 the same verb stands beside "predestined". Israel was chosen before it did anything (9:11).

decisions.choice: "whom he foreknew" describes the whole people
alternatives: it marks out a part of the people: those of Israel whom he foreknew
decisions.reason: Verse 1 asks about God's people as a whole, and the answer repeats its words. The clause gives the reason God will not reject them: he chose them. Verses 5-7 then speak of a remnant within the people.

decisions.choice: He knew them and chose them from the beginning
decisions.reason: Readable explains "foreknew" as the meaning decision describes it.

records.source: ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ἐν Ἠλίᾳ τί λέγει ἡ γραφή, ὡς ἐντυγχάνει τῷ θεῷ κατὰ τοῦ Ἰσραήλ;
records.gloss: Or not you know in Elijah what says the Scripture, how he pleads with the God against the Israel?
pieces: Or do you not know what Scripture says in the story of Elijah, how he appealed to God against Israel?

L.2: Or do you not know what the Scripture says in [the passage about] Elijah, how he pleads with God against Israel?

R.2: Do you remember what Scripture says in the story of Elijah? He complained to God about the people of Israel.

decisions.choice: in Elijah: in the passage that tells about Elijah
decisions.reason: Before chapters and verses existed, a passage was named by its subject, as Mark 12:26 says "at the bush" for the story of Moses at the burning bush. The story is 1 Kings 19.

decisions.choice: he appealed to God against Israel: he accused Israel before God
alternatives: he prayed to God for Israel
decisions.reason: The verb means to approach someone with a request; with "against" it means to bring a complaint. Elijah's words in verse 3 are an accusation.

decisions.choice: in the story of Elijah
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what "in Elijah" refers to.

decisions.choice: appealed (B); complained (R)
decisions.reason: The present tense of the Greek tells a past story vividly; English tells it in the past. "Intercedes" would suggest prayer on Israel's behalf.

records.source: Κύριε, τοὺς προφήτας σου ἀπέκτειναν, τὰ θυσιαστήριά σου κατέσκαψαν, κἀγὼ ὑπελείφθην μόνος, καὶ ζητοῦσιν τὴν ψυχήν μου.
records.gloss: Lord, the prophets of you they killed, the altars of you they tore down, and I was left alone, and they seek the life of me.
pieces: "Lord, they have killed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets and demolished {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars. I alone am left, and now they are trying to take my life."

L.3: "Lord, they have killed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets, they have torn down {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars, and I alone am left, and they are seeking my life."

R.3: "Lord, they have killed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} prophets. They have destroyed {{deity_pronoun:your|Your}} altars. I am the only one left, and now they want to kill me."

decisions.choice: 1 Kings 19:10 and 19:14
decisions.reason: Paul quotes Elijah's complaint in shortened form, putting the prophets before the altars and adding the address "Lord". In the Hebrew, Elijah speaks of the divine name just before: he has been zealous for the LORD, the God of hosts.

decisions.choice: they are seeking my life: they are trying to kill me
decisions.reason: To "seek someone's life" is a Hebrew way of saying "try to kill"; Jezebel had sworn to kill Elijah (1 Kings 19:2).

decisions.choice: trying to take my life (B); want to kill me (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable explain the idiom.

records.source: ἀλλὰ τί λέγει αὐτῷ ὁ χρηματισμός;
records.gloss: But what says to him the divine answer?
pieces: But what was God's answer to him?

L.4: But what does the divine answer say to him?

R.4: But what did God say to him in reply?

decisions.choice: the divine answer: a reply given by God
decisions.reason: The noun is used only here in the New Testament; the related verb is used of God warning or instructing people (Matthew 2:12, Hebrews 8:5). The answer in 1 Kings 19:18 is God's.

decisions.choice: God's answer
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name God as the one who answers, as the noun implies.

records.source: Κατέλιπον ἐμαυτῷ ἑπτακισχιλίους ἄνδρας, οἵτινες οὐκ ἔκαμψαν γόνυ τῇ Βάαλ.
records.gloss: I left to myself seven-thousand men, who not bent knee to the Baal.
pieces: "I have kept for {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} seven thousand {{gender:people|men}} who have not bent the knee to Baal."

L.4: "I have kept for {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}} seven thousand {{gender:people|men}} who have not bent [the] knee to Baal."

R.4: "I have kept seven thousand {{gender:people|men}} for {{deity_pronoun:myself|Myself}}. They have not bowed down to worship Baal."

decisions.choice: 1 Kings 19:18
decisions.reason: Paul gives God's answer freely. The Hebrew says "I will leave seven thousand in Israel"; Paul adds "for myself", stressing that God himself kept them faithful. In the Hebrew the answer is given by the LORD (the divine name, 1 Kings 19:15).

decisions.choice: people: the faithful Israelites, counted by heads
decisions.reason: The Greek word normally means men, but the Hebrew of 1 Kings 19:18 has no word for men, and Paul's point is the faithful remnant of Israel, not its males.

decisions.choice: bending the knee: worshiping
decisions.reason: Kneeling before a god was the act of worship (Isaiah 45:23). Baal was the Canaanite storm god whose worship Ahab and Jezebel promoted. The Greek puts a feminine article before the name (τῇ Βάαλ), as the old Greek translation sometimes does; this may reflect the Jewish custom of reading "shame" in place of the god's name.

decisions.choice: bowed down to worship
decisions.reason: Readable explains the gesture.

records.source: οὕτως οὖν καὶ ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ λεῖμμα κατ’ ἐκλογὴν χάριτος γέγονεν·
records.gloss: Thus then also in the now time a remnant according to election of grace has come to be;
pieces: In the same way, at the present time too there is a remnant, chosen by grace.

L.5: So then also in the present time there has come to be a remnant according to [the] election of grace.

R.5: It is the same today. Some of Israel are still left, a remnant whom God has chosen by {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} grace.

decisions.choice: remnant: the part of Israel that God keeps for himself
decisions.reason: The prophets spoke of a remnant of Israel that would survive judgment and return to God (Isaiah 10:20-22, quoted in 9:27). The seven thousand of Elijah's day were such a remnant; the Jews who now believe in Jesus are another.

decisions.choice: chosen by grace: a choice that comes from God's grace
alternatives: a choice that consists in grace
decisions.reason: "Election of grace" means God's choosing, which springs from grace and not from anything in the people chosen, as verse 6 explains.

decisions.choice: Some of Israel are still left, a remnant
decisions.reason: Readable says what a remnant is before using the word.

records.source: εἰ δὲ χάριτι, οὐκέτι ἐξ ἔργων, ἐπεὶ ἡ χάρις οὐκέτι γίνεται χάρις.
records.gloss: If and by grace, no longer from works, since the grace no longer becomes grace.
pieces: And if it is by grace, it does not come from works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

L.6: And if by grace, [it is] no longer from works, since [then] grace would no longer be grace.

R.6: And if God chose them by grace, then it was not because of what they did. If it were, grace would not really be grace.

decisions.choice: if it is by grace: if the remnant is chosen by grace
decisions.reason: The sentence leaves out its subject; it continues verse 5, where the remnant is chosen by grace.

decisions.choice: works: anything people do to earn God's choice
decisions.reason: Elsewhere in Romans "works" are often the works the law requires (3:20, 3:28), but here they stand against grace in general, as in 4:4-5 and 9:11-12.

decisions.choice: the sentence ends with "grace would no longer be grace"
alternatives: some later manuscripts add: "But if it is by works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work"
decisions.reason: The longer text is found in later manuscripts and in the King James Version; the oldest manuscripts do not have it. Reviewers must check the details against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: what they did
decisions.reason: Readable says what "works" means, as elsewhere in Romans and Galatians.

records.source: τί οὖν;
records.gloss: What then?
pieces: What then?

decisions.choice: What follows from this?
decisions.reason: Paul uses this short question to draw a conclusion from what he has said (3:9, 6:15).

decisions.choice: So what does this mean?
decisions.reason: Readable spells out the short question.

records.source: ὃ ἐπιζητεῖ Ἰσραήλ, τοῦτο οὐκ ἐπέτυχεν, ἡ δὲ ἐκλογὴ ἐπέτυχεν· οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ ἐπωρώθησαν, καθὼς γέγραπται· Ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς πνεῦμα κατανύξεως, ὀφθαλμοὺς τοῦ μὴ βλέπειν καὶ ὦτα τοῦ μὴ ἀκούειν, ἕως τῆς σήμερον ἡμέρας.
records.gloss: What is seeking Israel, this not it obtained, but the election obtained [it]; and the rest were hardened, \v 8 as it has been written: Gave to them the God a spirit of stupor, eyes the not to see and ears the not to hear, until the today day.
pieces: Israel did not obtain what it was seeking. Those God chose obtained it, but the rest were hardened,
as it is written, "God has given them a spirit of numbness, eyes that do not see and ears that do not hear, to this very day."

L.7: What Israel is seeking, this it did not obtain, but the elect obtained [it]; and the rest were hardened,
L.8: just as it is written, "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes [so as] not to see and ears [so as] not to hear, to this very day."

R.7: So the people of Israel did not find what they were looking for. Only those God chose found it. God made the rest of them stubborn.
R.8: As Scripture says, "God made their minds dull. He gave them eyes that cannot see and ears that cannot hear, and they are still like that today."

decisions.choice: what Israel seeks: righteousness, being right with God
decisions.reason: Paul has just said that Israel pursued righteousness but did not reach it (9:31, 10:3).

decisions.choice: the elect: those whom God chose
decisions.reason: The noun means "choice" or "election", but here it stands for the people chosen, the remnant of verse 5.

decisions.choice: were hardened: God made them unresponsive
decisions.reason: The passive verb does not name who hardened them, but the quotation that follows says God gave them a spirit of stupor, as in 9:18. Hardening is a picture of becoming unable to see or respond.

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 29:4 with Isaiah 29:10
decisions.reason: Paul joins Moses' words, "the LORD has not given you a heart to know, or eyes to see, or ears to hear, to this day" (Deuteronomy 29:4, 29:3 in Hebrew), with Isaiah 29:10, "the LORD has poured out on you a spirit of deep sleep". The Hebrew of both has the divine name; Paul writes "God".

decisions.choice: a spirit of stupor: a numbness that keeps them from understanding
decisions.reason: The old Greek translation of Isaiah 29:10 uses this phrase for the Hebrew "spirit of deep sleep". The word means a dazed numbness.

decisions.choice: those God chose
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable name the people meant.

decisions.choice: God made the rest of them stubborn
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who hardened them, as the meaning decision explains, and uses "stubborn" for the picture of hardening.

decisions.choice: As it is written (B); As Scripture says (R)
alternatives: just as it has been written
decisions.reason: "It is written" is the normal formula for quoting Scripture; Readable names Scripture, as in 1:17.

records.source: καὶ Δαυὶδ λέγει· Γενηθήτω ἡ τράπεζα αὐτῶν εἰς παγίδα καὶ εἰς θήραν καὶ εἰς σκάνδαλον καὶ εἰς ἀνταπόδομα αὐτοῖς, σκοτισθήτωσαν οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ αὐτῶν τοῦ μὴ βλέπειν, καὶ τὸν νῶτον αὐτῶν διὰ παντὸς σύγκαμψον.
records.gloss: And David says: Let become the table of them for a snare and for a trap and for a stumbling block and for a retribution to them, \v 10 let be darkened the eyes of them the not to see, and the back of them through all bend down.
pieces: And David says, "May their table turn into a snare and a net, a stumbling block and a just penalty for them.
May their eyes grow dark so that they cannot see, and keep their backs bent forever."

L.9: And David says, "Let their table become a snare and a trap and a stumbling block and a retribution to them;
L.10: let their eyes be darkened so as not to see, and bend their back continually."

R.9: And David says, "May the meals they enjoy become a trap that catches them. May they trip and fall and get what they deserve.
R.10: May their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see. Keep their backs bent low forever."

decisions.reason: Paul quotes Psalm 69:23-24 (68:23-24 in the old Greek translation) closely, from a psalm headed "Of David". The words "and a trap" are not in that psalm, and the order of the other nouns differs. The psalm is a prayer against those who persecute the righteous sufferer; the New Testament reads it of Jesus (John 2:17, 15:25; Romans 15:3).

decisions.choice: their table: the meals and good things they enjoy and rely on
alternatives: the law and its privileges, which became a trap for them
decisions.reason: In the psalm the table is the enemies' food and feasting, which is to turn against them. Paul does not say what the table stands for in Israel's case; the plain sense is the good things they enjoy becoming the means of their fall.

decisions.choice: a retribution: a fitting repayment
decisions.reason: The noun means a repayment, here a punishment that matches what was done.

decisions.choice: bend their back: bring them under a heavy load
alternatives: bowed down in grief or weakness
decisions.reason: A bent back is the posture of a slave or a person carrying a burden; it can also picture grief. The words continue the picture of darkened eyes: people weighed down and unable to look up.

decisions.choice: continually: for all time
decisions.reason: The phrase means "through everything", that is, all the time.

decisions.choice: May ...
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable express the Greek third-person commands as wishes, the usual English for a prayer of this kind.

decisions.choice: the meals they enjoy ... a trap ... trip and fall ... get what they deserve
alternatives: their table ... a snare and a trap ... a stumbling block ... a retribution
decisions.reason: Readable explains the picture of the table and gives the four nouns in plain words.

records.source: Λέγω οὖν, μὴ ἔπταισαν ἵνα πέσωσιν;
records.gloss: I say then, not they stumbled that they might fall?
pieces: So I ask: did they stumble so as to fall for good?

L.11: I say then, did they stumble so that they might fall?

R.11: So I ask this: When the people of Israel stumbled, did they fall and never get up again?

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no"
decisions.reason: As in verse 1, the negative particle expects a denial, which follows at once.

decisions.choice: stumble ... fall: trip up, or fall down for good
alternatives: two words for the same thing
decisions.reason: The contrast between the two verbs carries the point: Israel has stumbled (9:32-33), but has it fallen beyond recovery? The answer is no.

decisions.choice: so as to: with the result that
alternatives: in order that: was their fall God's purpose?
decisions.reason: The conjunction can express purpose or result. Paul's answer, which speaks of what their stumbling led to, fits either; "so as to" keeps both open.

decisions.choice: fall for good (B); fall and never get up again (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable bring out the contrast with "stumble", which the meaning decision describes.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable names who "they" are.

records.heading: Israel's stumbling and the Gentiles' salvation

records.source: μὴ γένοιτο· ἀλλὰ τῷ αὐτῶν παραπτώματι ἡ σωτηρία τοῖς ἔθνεσιν, εἰς τὸ παραζηλῶσαι αὐτούς.
records.gloss: Not may it be; but by the of them trespass the salvation to the Gentiles, for the to provoke to jealousy them.
pieces: Certainly not! Rather, through their wrongdoing salvation has come to the Gentiles, so that Israel would become jealous.

L.11: May it not be! But by their trespass salvation [has come] to the Gentiles, so as to make them jealous.

R.11: Of course not! Because they did wrong, salvation has come to people who are not Jews. That was meant to make the people of Israel jealous.

decisions.choice: the strongest possible denial
decisions.reason: μὴ γένοιτο, "may it not happen", is Paul's strongest way of rejecting a false conclusion (3:4, 6:2, 9:14; Galatians 2:17).

decisions.choice: trespass: a false step, a wrong
decisions.reason: The noun means a false step, continuing the picture of stumbling. Here it is Israel's refusal to believe in the Messiah (10:16-21).

decisions.choice: Deuteronomy 32:21
decisions.reason: Paul has just quoted God's words, "I will make you jealous by those who are not a nation" (10:19). Salvation coming to the Gentiles is meant to stir Israel to want it too.

decisions.choice: by their trespass: their trespass was the occasion for salvation to go out
decisions.reason: When Jews rejected the gospel, the apostles turned to the Gentiles (Acts 13:46, 28:28). Paul does not say Israel's sin saves anyone, but that God used it.

decisions.choice: Certainly not! (B); Of course not! (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use ordinary English for an emphatic no. "God forbid" adds a word for God that the Greek does not have.

decisions.choice: wrongdoing (B); they did wrong (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable use everyday words for the wrong step.

decisions.choice: Israel (B); the people of Israel (R)
decisions.reason: English "them" could seem to mean the Gentiles; Balanced and Readable name Israel.

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says what "Gentiles" means, as in 1:16.

records.source: εἰ δὲ τὸ παράπτωμα αὐτῶν πλοῦτος κόσμου καὶ τὸ ἥττημα αὐτῶν πλοῦτος ἐθνῶν, πόσῳ μᾶλλον τὸ πλήρωμα αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: If and the trespass of them riches of world and the loss of them riches of Gentiles, how much more the fullness of them.
pieces: Now if their wrongdoing means riches for the world, and their loss means riches for the Gentiles, how much greater riches their fullness will bring!

L.12: Now if their trespass [means] riches for [the] world, and their loss [means] riches for [the] Gentiles, how much more their fullness!

R.12: Their wrong step brought great blessing to the world. Their loss brought great blessing to people who are not Jews. So think how much greater the blessing will be when their full number is brought in!

decisions.choice: the world: humanity, the nations beyond Israel
decisions.reason: Parallel to "the Gentiles", the world here is the human race to whom the gospel now goes.

decisions.choice: their loss: their defeat or failure
alternatives: their reduction to a small number, in contrast with their "fullness"
decisions.reason: The noun means a defeat or loss. Set against "fullness", some take it to mean that Israel has been reduced to a remnant.

decisions.choice: their fullness: their full number, Israel restored as a whole
decisions.reason: The same word is used of "the full number of the Gentiles" in verse 25, and verse 26 says that all Israel will be saved. Paul looks forward to the time when Israel as a whole is brought in.

decisions.choice: how much more: an argument from the lesser to the greater
decisions.reason: If Israel's failure has brought such blessing, their restoration will bring far more, as verse 15 says.

decisions.choice: great blessing
decisions.reason: Readable says what the picture of riches means: spiritual blessing.

decisions.choice: when their full number is brought in
decisions.reason: Readable follows the meaning decision and uses the same wording as verse 25.

decisions.choice: people who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says what "Gentiles" means.

records.source: Ὑμῖν δὲ λέγω τοῖς ἔθνεσιν.
records.gloss: To you and I speak the Gentiles.
pieces: Now I am speaking to you who are Gentiles.

L.13: But I am speaking to you, the Gentiles.

R.13: Now I am speaking to you who are not Jews.

decisions.choice: the Gentile believers in Rome
decisions.reason: Paul turns to the Gentile believers among his readers. The church in Rome had both Jewish and Gentile members (1:13, 16:3-15), and here he warns the Gentiles against looking down on Israel.

decisions.choice: you who are not Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says what "Gentiles" means.

records.source: ἐφ’ ὅσον μὲν οὖν εἰμι ἐγὼ ἐθνῶν ἀπόστολος, τὴν διακονίαν μου δοξάζω, εἴ πως παραζηλώσω μου τὴν σάρκα καὶ σώσω τινὰς ἐξ αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: Inasmuch as indeed then am I of Gentiles apostle, the ministry of me I glorify, \v 14 if somehow I may provoke to jealousy of me the flesh and may save some of them.
pieces: So since I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I make much of my ministry,
in the hope that somehow I may make my own flesh and blood jealous and save some of them.

L.13: Inasmuch then as I am an apostle of [the] Gentiles, I glorify my ministry,
L.14: if somehow I may make my flesh jealous and save some of them.

R.13: God sent me as an apostle to people who are not Jews, so I make much of this work.
R.14: I hope that in some way I can make my own people, the Jews, jealous, and save some of them.

decisions.choice: I glorify: I honor my ministry and make the most of it
alternatives: I praise God for my ministry
decisions.reason: The verb usually means to give glory, but with "my ministry" as its object it means to hold it in honor and give it full weight, in the hope of the result verse 14 names.

decisions.choice: my flesh: my own people, my fellow Jews
decisions.reason: "Flesh" here means physical kinship, as in 9:3, "my kindred according to the flesh".

decisions.choice: save some: bring some to salvation through the gospel
decisions.reason: Paul speaks of saving people as the one who brings them the gospel, as in 1 Corinthians 9:22. Elsewhere it is God who saves (11:26).

decisions.choice: make much of
decisions.reason: "Glorify my ministry" sounds odd in English; Balanced and Readable give the sense described in the meaning decision.

decisions.choice: my own flesh and blood
decisions.reason: Balanced keeps the word "flesh" in a natural English phrase for kin.

decisions.choice: my own people, the Jews
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly who are meant.

decisions.choice: God sent me as an apostle to people who are not Jews
alternatives: I am an apostle of the Gentiles
decisions.reason: An apostle is one sent; Readable names God as the sender (1:1, 1:5).

records.source: εἰ γὰρ ἡ ἀποβολὴ αὐτῶν καταλλαγὴ κόσμου, τίς ἡ πρόσλημψις εἰ μὴ ζωὴ ἐκ νεκρῶν;
records.gloss: If for the rejection of them reconciliation of world, what the acceptance if not life from dead?
pieces: For if their rejection means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean? Nothing less than life from the dead!

L.15: For if their rejection [means the] reconciliation of [the] world, what [will their] acceptance [be] but life from [the] dead?

R.15: When God set them aside, the world was brought back to God and made friends with {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. So what will it be like when God takes them back? It will be life from the dead!

decisions.choice: their rejection: God's setting them aside
decisions.reason: The phrase could mean that Israel rejected or that Israel was rejected. The matching phrase "their acceptance" most naturally means God accepting them, so "their rejection" is God's setting them aside for a time. This does not contradict verses 1-2: it is not a final casting off.

decisions.choice: the reconciliation of the world: people of all nations brought back into peace with God
decisions.reason: Reconciliation means ending hostility and restoring friendship (5:10-11; 2 Corinthians 5:18-20). "The world" is humanity beyond Israel.

decisions.choice: life from the dead: something as great as resurrection
alternatives: the resurrection of the dead at the end of the age
a picture of new spiritual life for the world
decisions.reason: Paul may mean that Israel's acceptance will come with the final resurrection, or he may be using resurrection as a picture of an overwhelming blessing. The words allow both, and the translation keeps them as they are.

decisions.choice: what will their acceptance mean? Nothing less than life from the dead!
alternatives: what will their acceptance be but life from the dead?
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the question "what ... if not" into a question and an answer.

decisions.choice: When God set them aside, the world was brought back to God and made friends with him
alternatives: their rejection is the reconciliation of the world
decisions.reason: Readable names God, as the meaning decision explains, and says what reconciliation is.

records.source: εἰ δὲ ἡ ἀπαρχὴ ἁγία, καὶ τὸ φύραμα· καὶ εἰ ἡ ῥίζα ἁγία, καὶ οἱ κλάδοι.
records.gloss: If and the firstfruit holy, also the lump; and if the root holy, also the branches.
pieces: If the portion of dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole batch; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.

L.16: Now if the firstfruit [is] holy, so [is] the lump; and if the root [is] holy, so [are] the branches.

R.16: If the first piece of dough is offered to God and is holy, the whole batch of dough is holy too. And if the root of a tree is holy, so are its branches.

decisions.choice: the offering of the first of the dough, Numbers 15:17-21
decisions.reason: Israel was to offer to God a cake from the first of its dough. Once that part was given, the whole batch could be used, as belonging to God.

decisions.choice: holy: set apart for God, belonging to him
decisions.reason: Holiness here is belonging to God, not moral goodness.

decisions.choice: the firstfruits and the root: Israel's forefathers, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
alternatives: the first Jewish believers in Jesus
decisions.reason: Verse 28 says Israel is loved "because of the fathers", which suggests the root is the patriarchs, to whom the promises were made. Some take the firstfruits to be the Jewish believers (the remnant) and the root to be the patriarchs.

decisions.choice: the portion of dough offered as firstfruits (B); the first piece of dough is offered to God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what the firstfruit is, since "lump" refers to dough.

records.source: Εἰ δέ τινες τῶν κλάδων ἐξεκλάσθησαν, σὺ δὲ ἀγριέλαιος ὢν ἐνεκεντρίσθης ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ συγκοινωνὸς τῆς ῥίζης τῆς πιότητος τῆς ἐλαίας ἐγένου, μὴ κατακαυχῶ τῶν κλάδων· εἰ δὲ κατακαυχᾶσαι, οὐ σὺ τὴν ῥίζαν βαστάζεις ἀλλὰ ἡ ῥίζα σέ.
records.gloss: If but some of the branches were broken off, and you a wild olive being were grafted in among them and fellow-sharer of the root of the richness of the olive tree became, \v 18 not boast over the branches; if but you boast, not you the root support but the root you.
pieces: Now if some of the branches were broken off, and you, though a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among them and now share in the rich root of the olive tree,
do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, remember: you do not hold up the root; the root holds you up.

L.17: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them and became a sharer of the root of the richness of the olive tree,
L.18: do not boast over the branches; but if you do boast, [remember that] it is not you [who] support the root, but the root [supports] you.

R.17: Some of the branches of the olive tree were broken off. You are like a shoot from a wild olive tree that was joined onto the tree among the other branches. Now you share the rich sap that comes up from its root.
R.18: So do not think you are better than the natural branches. If you are tempted to boast, remember this: You do not hold up the root. The root holds you up.

decisions.choice: Israel as God's olive tree
decisions.reason: The prophets called Israel an olive tree planted by God (Jeremiah 11:16, Hosea 14:6). The broken branches are unbelieving Israelites; the wild shoot is the Gentile believer.

decisions.choice: you: one Gentile believer, addressed as an example
decisions.reason: Paul speaks to an imagined Gentile listener in the singular, as he does in 2:1-5 and 9:19-20, to warn all the Gentile believers.

decisions.choice: grafting a wild shoot into a cultivated tree
decisions.reason: Farmers grafted cultivated shoots onto wild stock, not the reverse; Paul himself says the grafting he describes is "contrary to nature" (verse 24). The unusual picture shows that the Gentiles' place is God's gift.

decisions.choice: "the root of the richness": the rich root
alternatives: "the root and the richness of the olive tree"
"the richness of the olive tree", without "the root"
decisions.reason: The oldest manuscripts have two genitives in a row, "of the root of the richness"; some manuscripts add "and" between them, and others leave out "the root". The meaning is the same. Reviewers must check the details against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: richness: the rich sap that nourishes the tree
decisions.reason: The word means fatness; the olive tree's richness is the life it draws from its root and gives to its branches.

decisions.choice: You are like a shoot from a wild olive tree that was joined onto the tree among the other branches
alternatives: you, being a wild olive, were grafted in among them
decisions.reason: Readable makes the comparison explicit and explains grafting.

decisions.choice: do not think you are better than the natural branches
alternatives: do not boast over the branches
decisions.reason: Readable gives the sense of boasting over others: looking down on them. The branches are those that belong to the tree by nature (verse 21).

records.heading: The olive tree and its branches

records.source: ἐρεῖς οὖν· Ἐξεκλάσθησαν κλάδοι ἵνα ἐγὼ ἐγκεντρισθῶ.
records.gloss: You will say then: Were broken off branches that I might be grafted in.
pieces: Then you will say, "Branches were broken off to let me be grafted in."

L.19: You will say then, "Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in."

R.19: Then you might say, "God broke those branches off to make room for me."

decisions.choice: so that: the Gentile's claim that God's purpose was to make room for him
decisions.reason: The imagined speaker takes the breaking off as having been done for his sake. Paul grants the fact in verse 20 but not the pride behind it.

decisions.choice: God broke those branches off to make room for me
alternatives: branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one who broke the branches off, as verse 21 implies, and says what grafting in means for the speaker.

records.source: καλῶς· τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ ἐξεκλάσθησαν, σὺ δὲ τῇ πίστει ἕστηκας.
records.gloss: Well; by the unbelief they were broken off, but you by the faith stand.
pieces: That is true. They were broken off because of their unbelief, but you stand firm by faith.

L.20: Well [said]; they were broken off because of unbelief, but you stand by faith.

R.20: That is true. But they were broken off because they did not believe. And you are still there only because of your faith.

decisions.choice: Well said: granted, that is true as far as it goes
decisions.reason: Paul agrees with the fact but goes on to correct the conclusion the speaker draws from it.

decisions.choice: unbelief: not believing
decisions.reason: Set against "faith" in the same sentence, this is the unbelief of 10:16-21: refusing to believe the gospel.

decisions.choice: because of unbelief ... by faith
decisions.reason: The two datives give the cause on each side: unbelief led to the branches being broken off, and faith is how the Gentile stands.

decisions.choice: stand firm (B); are still there (R)
decisions.reason: Standing means keeping one's place on the tree; Readable continues the picture.

decisions.choice: only because of your faith
decisions.reason: Readable brings out the contrast with the broken branches: faith, not anything else, keeps the Gentile on the tree.

records.source: μὴ ὑψηλὰ φρόνει, ἀλλὰ φοβοῦ·
records.gloss: Not high things be minded, but fear;
pieces: Do not be proud, but fear.

L.20: Do not think lofty [thoughts], but fear.

R.20: So do not be proud. Fear God instead.

decisions.choice: do not think high thoughts: do not be proud
decisions.reason: To "think high things" means to be arrogant, as in 12:16.

decisions.choice: fear: a reverent fear of God and his judgment
decisions.reason: The next verse gives the reason: God did not spare the natural branches. This is the fear that keeps a person humble before God, not general anxiety.

decisions.choice: Fear God
decisions.reason: Readable names God as the one to be feared, as verse 21 makes clear.

records.source: εἰ γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τῶν κατὰ φύσιν κλάδων οὐκ ἐφείσατο, οὐδὲ σοῦ φείσεται.
records.gloss: If for the God the according to nature branches not spared, neither you will he spare.
pieces: For if God did not spare the branches that grew naturally on the tree, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will not spare you either.

L.21: For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} spare you.

R.21: God did not spare the branches that belonged to the tree by nature. So if you become proud, {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will not spare you either.

decisions.choice: if God did not spare: since he did not spare
decisions.reason: The "if" states a fact Paul has already described: the natural branches were broken off.

decisions.choice: the natural branches: Israelites by birth
decisions.reason: Branches that grew on the tree "by nature" are Jews, members of Israel by descent, in contrast to the grafted wild shoot.

decisions.choice: neither will he spare you
alternatives: some manuscripts add "perhaps": "perhaps he will not spare you either"
decisions.reason: A number of early manuscripts soften the warning with a word meaning "perhaps"; other early manuscripts do not have it. Reviewers must check the details against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: So if you become proud
decisions.reason: Readable states the condition the warning assumes, from verse 20 ("do not be proud") and verse 22 ("if you continue in his kindness").

records.source: ἴδε οὖν χρηστότητα καὶ ἀποτομίαν θεοῦ· ἐπὶ μὲν τοὺς πεσόντας ἀποτομία, ἐπὶ δὲ σὲ χρηστότης θεοῦ, ἐὰν ἐπιμένῃς τῇ χρηστότητι, ἐπεὶ καὶ σὺ ἐκκοπήσῃ.
records.gloss: See then kindness and severity of God; upon on the one hand the having fallen severity, upon on the other hand you kindness of God, if you continue in the kindness, otherwise also you will be cut off.
pieces: Notice, then, both the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but God's kindness toward you, as long as you continue in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} kindness. Otherwise you too will be cut off.

L.22: See then [the] kindness and severity of God: on those who fell, severity, but on you, God's kindness, if you continue in [that] kindness; otherwise you too will be cut off.

R.22: So think about how kind God is, and also how severe {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is. He was severe with those who fell. But {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} is kind to you, as long as you keep living in {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} kindness. If you do not, you will be cut off too.

decisions.choice: kindness: God's goodness and generosity
decisions.reason: The same word is used of God's kindness that leads to repentance in 2:4.

decisions.choice: severity: sternness in judgment
decisions.reason: The word comes from a verb meaning "to cut off" and suits the picture of branches cut from the tree.

decisions.choice: continue in his kindness: keep relying on God's kindness, by faith
decisions.reason: The kindness is God's, named twice just before. To continue in it is to keep standing by faith (verse 20), not trusting one's own standing.

decisions.choice: keep living in his kindness
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plain verb for remaining in God's kindness.

records.source: κἀκεῖνοι δέ, ἐὰν μὴ ἐπιμένωσι τῇ ἀπιστίᾳ, ἐγκεντρισθήσονται· δυνατὸς γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θεὸς πάλιν ἐγκεντρίσαι αὐτούς.
records.gloss: And those also, if not they continue in the unbelief, will be grafted in; able for is the God again to graft in them.
pieces: And they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God has the power to graft them back in.

L.23: And they also, if they do not continue in unbelief, will be grafted in; for God is able to graft them in again.

R.23: And if the people of Israel stop refusing to believe, they will be joined to the tree again. God has the power to put them back in.

decisions.choice: if they do not continue in unbelief: their return depends on faith
decisions.reason: The same condition holds for both sides: Gentiles stand by faith (verse 20), and Israelites who come to faith will be grafted back in.

decisions.choice: God is able: God has the power to do it
decisions.reason: Paul rests his hope on God's power, as Abraham did (4:21). Restoring cut-off branches is beyond what a farmer could do, but not beyond God.

decisions.choice: stop refusing to believe
decisions.reason: Readable turns the negative condition into a plain verb.

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable names who "they" are.

records.source: εἰ γὰρ σὺ ἐκ τῆς κατὰ φύσιν ἐξεκόπης ἀγριελαίου καὶ παρὰ φύσιν ἐνεκεντρίσθης εἰς καλλιέλαιον, πόσῳ μᾶλλον οὗτοι οἱ κατὰ φύσιν ἐγκεντρισθήσονται τῇ ἰδίᾳ ἐλαίᾳ.
records.gloss: If for you out of the according to nature were cut off wild olive and contrary to nature were grafted into cultivated olive, how much more these the according to nature will be grafted into the own olive tree.
pieces: After all, if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree and grafted, against nature, into a cultivated olive tree, how much more readily will these natural branches be grafted back into their own olive tree!

L.24: For if you were cut out of the olive tree that is wild by nature, and contrary to nature were grafted into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural [branches], be grafted into their own olive tree!

R.24: You were cut from a wild olive tree, where you grew naturally. Then, against the way things usually grow, you were joined to a garden olive tree. The natural branches belong to that tree. So it will be even easier for God to join them back to their own tree!

decisions.choice: contrary to nature: against the usual way of things
decisions.reason: Here the phrase describes unusual gardening, not wrongdoing: a wild shoot does not normally grow on a cultivated tree. Compare the different use in 1:26.

decisions.choice: how much more: an argument from the harder to the easier
decisions.reason: If God did the unusual thing for the Gentiles, restoring Israel to its own tree is a smaller step.

decisions.choice: wild olive and cultivated olive
decisions.reason: The wild olive bears little useful fruit; the cultivated olive was one of the main crops of the land. The picture stresses that the Gentiles have received what was not theirs by nature.

decisions.choice: how much more readily (B); even easier for God (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say in what way it is "more": easier. Readable names God as the one who grafts, as verse 23 says.

decisions.choice: garden olive tree
decisions.reason: Readable uses an everyday word for a tree that people plant and tend.

records.source: Οὐ γὰρ θέλω ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοί, τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο, ἵνα μὴ ἦτε ἑαυτοῖς φρόνιμοι, ὅτι πώρωσις ἀπὸ μέρους τῷ Ἰσραὴλ γέγονεν ἄχρι οὗ τὸ πλήρωμα τῶν ἐθνῶν εἰσέλθῃ, καὶ οὕτως πᾶς Ἰσραὴλ σωθήσεται· καθὼς γέγραπται· Ἥξει ἐκ Σιὼν ὁ ῥυόμενος, ἀποστρέψει ἀσεβείας ἀπὸ Ἰακώβ.
records.gloss: Not for I want you to be ignorant, brothers, of the mystery this, that not you be in yourselves wise, that a hardening in part to the Israel has happened until which the fullness of the Gentiles may come in, \v 26 and so all Israel will be saved; as it has been written: Will come out of Zion the delivering [one], he will turn away ungodliness from Jacob.
pieces: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I want you to understand this mystery, so that you will not think yourselves wise: a hardening has come upon part of Israel until the full number of the Gentiles comes in.
And in this way all Israel will be saved. As it is written, "Out of Zion will come the Deliverer; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will turn ungodliness away from Jacob."

L.25: For I do not want you to be ignorant, {{gender:brothers and sisters|brothers}}, of this mystery, so that you may not be wise in your own [eyes]: that a hardening in part has come to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in,
L.26: and in this way all Israel will be saved, just as it is written, "The Deliverer will come out of Zion; {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} will turn away ungodliness from Jacob."

R.25: {{gender:Brothers and sisters|Brothers}}, I want you to know a secret that God has now made known. Then you will not think you are wiser than you are. Part of Israel has been made stubborn, but only until the full number of people who are not Jews has come in.
R.26: And in this way all Israel will be saved. As Scripture says, "The One who rescues will come from Zion. He will turn the people of Jacob away from their ungodly ways."

decisions.choice: mystery: a part of God's plan once hidden and now made known
decisions.reason: In Paul a mystery is not a puzzle but a truth God has revealed (16:25-26; 1 Corinthians 2:7-10). Here it is the order of events in God's plan for Israel and the nations.

decisions.choice: a hardening in part: part of Israel is hardened
alternatives: a partial hardening of all Israel
decisions.reason: Verses 5-7 say that a remnant believes and "the rest were hardened", so the phrase most likely means that the hardening has come upon a part of Israel.

decisions.choice: the full number of the Gentiles: all the Gentiles God intends to bring in
decisions.reason: "Come in" is used of entering the kingdom of God (Matthew 7:13, Mark 9:47), and "fullness" here is the complete number, as in verse 12.

decisions.choice: in this way: by this process
alternatives: and then: after the Gentiles have come in
decisions.reason: The word normally means "in this way", referring to the process just described: hardening, the Gentiles coming in, Israel's jealousy. A time sense, "and then", is less usual but fits the "until" before it.

decisions.choice: all Israel: the people of Israel as a whole
alternatives: all God's people, Jews and Gentiles together (compare Galatians 6:16)
the full number of the believing remnant over time
decisions.reason: In this chapter "Israel" has meant the Jewish people (verses 1, 2, 7, 25), set against the Gentiles. Paul most likely means that Israel as a people will be saved at the end, as "all Israel" is used in the Old Testament of the nation as a whole (1 Samuel 7:5) without counting every member. Others read it as the church or the remnant.

decisions.choice: Isaiah 59:20 with Isaiah 27:9
decisions.reason: Paul quotes Isaiah 59:20 in a form close to the old Greek translation, which says the Redeemer will come "for the sake of Zion" and turn away ungodliness from Jacob. The Hebrew says he will come "to Zion", to those in Jacob who turn from sin, "declares the LORD" (the divine name). Paul writes "from Zion". The next line joins Isaiah 27:9, quoted in verse 27.

decisions.choice: the Deliverer: the one who rescues, most likely Christ
decisions.reason: In Isaiah the Redeemer is God. Paul calls Jesus the one "who rescues us from the coming wrath" with the same verb (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and most likely means Christ at his coming.

decisions.choice: I want you to understand
alternatives: I do not want you to be ignorant
decisions.reason: Balanced turns the double negative into a positive statement, as English normally does.

decisions.choice: a secret that God has now made known
decisions.reason: Readable explains "mystery" as the meaning decision describes it.

decisions.choice: Part of Israel has been made stubborn
alternatives: a hardening in part has come to Israel
decisions.reason: Readable uses "stubborn" for the picture of hardening, as in verse 7.

decisions.choice: As it is written (B); As Scripture says (R)
alternatives: just as it has been written
decisions.reason: "It is written" is the normal formula for quoting Scripture; Readable names Scripture.

records.heading: All Israel will be saved

records.source: καὶ αὕτη αὐτοῖς ἡ παρ’ ἐμοῦ διαθήκη, ὅταν ἀφέλωμαι τὰς ἁμαρτίας αὐτῶν.
records.gloss: And this to them the from me covenant, when I take away the sins of them.
pieces: "And this will be {{deity_pronoun:my|My}} covenant with them, when I take their sins away."

L.27: "And this [is] the covenant from {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} with them, when I take away their sins."

R.27: "This is the covenant I will make with them when I take away their sins."

decisions.choice: Isaiah 59:21 with Isaiah 27:9
decisions.reason: The first line comes from Isaiah 59:21, "This is my covenant with them, says the LORD" (the divine name in the Hebrew). The second comes from Isaiah 27:9, "when I take away his sin". The promise recalls the new covenant of Jeremiah 31:33-34, in which God forgives his people's sins.

decisions.choice: this will be my covenant: the clause has no verb, and points to the future
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb. Since the Deliverer "will come" and God will take away their sins, the covenant is one God will carry out.

decisions.choice: covenant: God's binding commitment to his people
decisions.reason: The covenant comes "from me": God makes it and keeps it.

decisions.choice: will be (B); I will make (R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable supply a verb in the future, following the meaning decision.

records.source: κατὰ μὲν τὸ εὐαγγέλιον ἐχθροὶ δι’ ὑμᾶς, κατὰ δὲ τὴν ἐκλογὴν ἀγαπητοὶ διὰ τοὺς πατέρας·
records.gloss: According to on the one hand the gospel enemies on account of you, according to on the other hand the election beloved on account of the fathers;
pieces: As far as the gospel is concerned, they are enemies for your sake; but as far as God's choice is concerned, they are loved because of the patriarchs.

L.28: As regards the gospel, [they are] enemies for your sake; but as regards the election, [they are] beloved for the sake of the fathers.

R.28: When it comes to the good news, they are now God's enemies, and that has been for your good. But God chose them, and {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} still loves them because of their ancestors Abraham, Isaac and Jacob.

decisions.choice: enemies: treated by God as enemies
alternatives: hostile to the gospel and to Paul's Gentile readers
decisions.reason: The word stands opposite "beloved", which means loved by God, so "enemies" most likely means that, for now, they stand opposed to God, as in 5:10. The other reading takes it of their hostility to the gospel.

decisions.choice: for your sake: for the benefit of you Gentiles
decisions.reason: As verses 11-12 and 15 say, Israel's unbelief opened the way for the gospel to reach the Gentiles.

decisions.choice: the election: God's choice of Israel
decisions.reason: This is God's choosing of Israel as his people (9:11), which still stands.

decisions.choice: the fathers: the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
decisions.reason: God loved Israel and chose it because of his love for its forefathers and his promises to them (Deuteronomy 7:8, 10:15; Romans 9:5).

decisions.choice: God's enemies
decisions.reason: Readable names whose enemies they are, following the meaning decision.

decisions.choice: their ancestors Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
decisions.reason: Readable names the patriarchs.

decisions.choice: God's choice
decisions.reason: Balanced says whose choice it is.

records.source: ἀμεταμέλητα γὰρ τὰ χαρίσματα καὶ ἡ κλῆσις τοῦ θεοῦ.
records.gloss: Irrevocable for the gifts and the calling of the God.
pieces: For the gifts and the call of God can never be taken back.

L.29: For the gifts and the calling of God [are] irrevocable.

R.29: God never changes {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} mind about the gifts {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} gives or about the people {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} calls.

decisions.choice: irrevocable: not regretted, never taken back
decisions.reason: The word means "without regret": God does not change his mind about what he has given (compare Numbers 23:19).

decisions.choice: the gifts and the calling: the privileges God gave Israel and his call of Israel to be his people
decisions.reason: Paul lists Israel's gifts in 9:4-5: adoption, glory, covenants, law, worship, promises. The calling is God's choice of Israel, the "election" of verse 28.

decisions.choice: God never changes his mind about
decisions.reason: Readable explains the word with a plain phrase.

records.source: ὥσπερ γὰρ ὑμεῖς ποτε ἠπειθήσατε τῷ θεῷ, νῦν δὲ ἠλεήθητε τῇ τούτων ἀπειθείᾳ, οὕτως καὶ οὗτοι νῦν ἠπείθησαν τῷ ὑμετέρῳ ἐλέει ἵνα καὶ αὐτοὶ νῦν ἐλεηθῶσιν·
records.gloss: Just as for you once disobeyed the God, now but received mercy by the of these disobedience, \v 31 so also these now disobeyed the your mercy so that also they now may receive mercy;
pieces: Once you were disobedient to God, but now you have been shown mercy because of their disobedience.
In the same way they have now been disobedient, so that by the mercy God has shown you, they too may now be shown mercy.

L.30: For just as you once were disobedient to God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience,
L.31: so these also have now been disobedient, for the mercy [shown] to you, so that they too may now receive mercy.

R.30: At one time you did not obey God. But now God has shown you mercy, because the people of Israel did not obey.
R.31: In the same way, they have now refused to obey, so that they too may now receive mercy because of the mercy God has shown you.

decisions.choice: disobey: refuse to obey, especially by not believing
decisions.reason: In Romans this verb is used of refusing the gospel (10:21, 15:31), so it includes unbelief.

decisions.choice: by the mercy shown to you goes with what follows: so that, through the mercy shown to you, they too may receive mercy
alternatives: it goes with what comes before: they have been disobedient because of the mercy shown to you
decisions.reason: In Greek the phrase stands before "so that", which suggests the second reading and matches "because of their disobedience" in verse 30. But Paul has already said that mercy to the Gentiles is meant to make Israel jealous and so bring them to mercy (verses 11 and 14), which fits the first. The Literal level keeps the Greek order.

decisions.choice: they too may now receive mercy
alternatives: some manuscripts leave out the second "now"
a few manuscripts read "later" in its place
decisions.reason: Early manuscripts are divided over the second "now"; the SBLGNT includes it. With it, Paul sees Israel's mercy as part of the present time. Reviewers must check the details against the SBLGNT apparatus.

decisions.choice: In the same way
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable split the long comparison into two sentences and join them with "In the same way".

decisions.choice: the people of Israel
decisions.reason: Readable names who "these" are.

decisions.choice: the mercy God has shown you
decisions.reason: "Your mercy" means the mercy shown to you, not mercy you show; Balanced and Readable say so.

records.source: συνέκλεισεν γὰρ ὁ θεὸς τοὺς πάντας εἰς ἀπείθειαν ἵνα τοὺς πάντας ἐλεήσῃ.
records.gloss: Shut up together for the God the all into disobedience so that the all he may have mercy on.
pieces: For God has locked everyone up together in disobedience, so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} may show mercy to everyone.

L.32: For God has shut up all in disobedience, so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} may have mercy on all.

R.32: God has put everyone in the prison of disobedience, so that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} can show mercy to everyone.

decisions.choice: shut up: imprison, lock in
decisions.reason: The verb means to shut in on all sides, like fish in a net or prisoners in a cell. Paul uses it the same way in Galatians 3:22.

decisions.choice: all: both Jews and Gentiles, all people without distinction
alternatives: every individual, all of whom will finally receive mercy
decisions.reason: Verses 30-31 have spoken of two groups, Gentiles and Jews, both disobedient and both shown mercy. The point is that no one is shown mercy on any other basis. Some read "all" as a promise that every person will be saved; elsewhere Romans speaks of judgment for those who refuse God (2:5-8).

decisions.choice: so that: God's purpose
decisions.reason: The aim of shutting everyone up in disobedience is mercy: no one can come to God except by mercy.

decisions.choice: put everyone in the prison of disobedience
decisions.reason: Readable keeps the picture of the verb and makes it plain.

records.source: Ὦ βάθος πλούτου καὶ σοφίας καὶ γνώσεως θεοῦ· ὡς ἀνεξεραύνητα τὰ κρίματα αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀνεξιχνίαστοι αἱ ὁδοὶ αὐτοῦ.
records.gloss: O depth of riches and of wisdom and of knowledge of God; how unsearchable the judgments of him and untraceable the ways of him.
pieces: How deep are the riches and the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How impossible to search out {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} judgments, and how impossible to trace {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} ways!

L.33: O [the] depth of [the] riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable [are] {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} judgments and untraceable {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} ways!

R.33: How great God's riches are! How deep {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} wisdom and knowledge are! No one can fully understand {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} decisions. No one can trace the paths {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} takes.

decisions.choice: three things are deep: God's riches, God's wisdom and God's knowledge
alternatives: the depth of the riches of God's wisdom and knowledge
decisions.reason: The three nouns are joined by "and ... and", so most likely each is its own subject of praise. The riches would be the riches of God's mercy (2:4, 9:23, 10:12). The other reading takes riches as describing the wisdom and knowledge.

decisions.choice: judgments: God's decisions
decisions.reason: The word here means the decisions God makes in governing the world and history, as the chapter has described them.

decisions.choice: Job 11:7-8 and Isaiah 55:8-9
decisions.reason: Paul's praise echoes the Old Testament theme that no one can search out the depths of God (Job 11:7-8) or match his thoughts and ways (Isaiah 55:8-9).

decisions.choice: No one can trace the paths he takes
decisions.reason: Readable turns the adjective into a plain sentence; the word means a track that cannot be followed.

records.heading: Praise to God's wisdom

records.source: Τίς γὰρ ἔγνω νοῦν κυρίου;
records.gloss: Who for has known mind of Lord?
pieces: For "who has known the mind of the Lord?"

L.34: For "who has known [the] mind of [the] Lord?"

R.34: As Scripture says, "Who has ever known what the Lord is thinking?"

decisions.choice: Isaiah 40:13
decisions.reason: Paul quotes the old Greek translation of Isaiah 40:13, as he does in 1 Corinthians 2:16. The Hebrew reads "Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD?", with the divine name; the Greek has "Lord". The quotation continues in the next sentence.

decisions.choice: mind: God's thoughts and purposes
decisions.reason: The question means that no one knows God's plans unless he reveals them.

decisions.choice: As Scripture says
decisions.reason: Readable tells the reader that a quotation follows, as the meaning decision explains.

records.source: ἢ τίς σύμβουλος αὐτοῦ ἐγένετο;
records.gloss: Or who counselor of him has become?
pieces: "Or who has been {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} counselor?"

decisions.choice: Isaiah 40:13, continued
decisions.reason: This is the second line of Isaiah 40:13; the Hebrew asks who has instructed the LORD as his counselor.

decisions.choice: given him advice
decisions.reason: Readable uses a plain verb.

records.source: ἢ τίς προέδωκεν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἀνταποδοθήσεται αὐτῷ;
records.gloss: Or who has first given to him, and it will be repaid to him?
pieces: "Or who has given {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} anything first and must be paid back?"

L.35: "Or who has first given to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}, and it will be repaid to him?"

R.35: "Has anyone ever given God a gift, so that God must pay them back?"

decisions.reason: The words are close to the Hebrew of Job 41:11 (41:3 in Hebrew), where God says, "Who has first given to me, that I should repay him?" The old Greek translation of that verse is quite different. In Job the divine name is not in this line.

decisions.choice: a question that expects the answer "no one"
decisions.reason: God owes nothing to anyone; everything he gives is grace (4:4, 11:6).

decisions.choice: God ... God must pay them back
alternatives: him ... it will be repaid to him
decisions.reason: Readable names God for both pronouns. The giver is "them", an English pronoun for one person of either sex.

records.source: ὅτι ἐξ αὐτοῦ καὶ δι’ αὐτοῦ καὶ εἰς αὐτὸν τὰ πάντα· αὐτῷ ἡ δόξα εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας, ἀμήν.
records.gloss: Because from him and through him and to him the all things; to him the glory to the ages, amen.
pieces: For all things are from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. To {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} be glory forever! Amen.

L.36: For from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and to {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [are] all things. To {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} [be] the glory forever. Amen.

R.36: Everything comes from {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Everything exists through {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}} and for {{deity_pronoun:him|Him}}. Let all glory be {{deity_pronoun:his|His}} forever! Amen.

decisions.choice: from him, through him, to him: God is the source, the means and the goal of all things
decisions.reason: The three prepositions say that all things come from God, exist by his working, and lead back to him (compare 1 Corinthians 8:6).

decisions.choice: to him be the glory: a wish or prayer
alternatives: to him is the glory: a statement
decisions.reason: The Greek has no verb. A doxology like this is normally a prayer that God will be glorified, as in 16:27 and Galatians 1:5.

decisions.choice: to the ages: forever
decisions.reason: "To the ages" is a Greek way of saying "forever".

decisions.choice: for him
decisions.reason: English says "for him" for the goal or purpose of something.

decisions.choice: Let all glory be his
decisions.reason: Readable puts the prayer in plain words, as the meaning decision describes it.
